text:
## Node.js 27.0.0 alpha : Node.js inaugure sa nouvelle politique de release 

 Soumis par francoistonic le ven, 30 Oct 2026 - 08:55 

 

Avec la version 27, Node.js lance son nouveau rythme de mise à jour. Désormais, une seule version majeure sera distribuée chaque année. Et chaque version est de facto une version LTS avec un support de 30 mois.

La version 27.x.x correspond à 2027, la 28 à 2028, etc. 

La version 27.0.0 rentre en phase alpha. Elle promet plusieurs changements importants :

- nouvelle version de V8 avec intégration de nouvelles fonctions : `Math.sumPrecise()`, `Intl.Locale.prototype.variants`, `Iterator.prototype.join()`, `Iterator.prototype.includes()`, `Iterator.zip()` and `Iterator.zipKeyed()`.
- OpenSSL 4.1
- npm 12.1

Note de version : https://nodejs.org/en/blog/release/v27.0.0-alpha.0.0.0

## Node.js 26.13.00 : passage en LTS, pas de nouveautés 

 Soumis par francoistonic le jeu, 29 Oct 2026 - 10:08 

 

Le projet Node.js annonce la disponibilité de la version 26.13.0 "Lithium". Cette version marque la transition de la branche 26.x vers un support LTS jusqu'en avril 2029. 

La seule modification par rapport à la précédente version stable est la mise à jour des métadonnées (ex. objet process.release).

Annonce : https://nodejs.org/en/blog/release/v26.13.0

title: Node.js 27 Alpha Is a Preview of More Predictable Runtimes
text:
Node.js 27 Alpha Is a Preview of More Predictable Runtimes

# Node.js 27 Alpha Is a Preview of More Predictable Runtimes

 WS Written by Shaik Sai Meera Editorial Team November 13, 2026 6 mins read 

Published: 13 November 2026 (IST) New major versions of Node.js are often described as a pile of changes for maintainers to scan later. The first Node.js 27 alpha points to a more useful story:…

Published: 13 November 2026 (IST)

New major versions of Node.js are often described as a pile of changes for maintainers to scan later. The first Node.js 27 alpha points to a more useful story: several low-level improvements are aimed at making long-running services, network clients, certificate workflows, and startup behavior easier to reason about. The release is still an alpha, so it is not a drop-in recommendation for production. But it is an early signal about where the runtime is heading.

The official Node.js release announcement lists changes across child processes, crypto, DNS, HTTP, the single executable application (SEA) system, and workers. Taken together, they are less about one headline feature and more about reducing ambiguity at the edges of application behavior.

...

Alpha releases are where platform teams can see upcoming interfaces before they become stable commitments. They are useful for compatibility testing, library authors, and developers who want to influence feedback. They are also deliberately unfinished. APIs can change, bugs are expected, and an alpha runtime should be isolated from production traffic.

That makes Node.js 27 a planning signal, not an upgrade command. A team can use it to identify code that may benefit from the new behavior, build a small test matrix, and discover assumptions before a later beta or stable release arrives.

...

Node.js 27 alpha is interesting because its changes connect application behavior to operational predictability. Clearer timeout outcomes, more explicit certificate handling, less duplicated DNS work, more deliberate HTTP parsing, and better startup primitives all address places where small ambiguities become expensive at scale.

title: Node.js 26 'Lithium' Goes LTS: Temporal Ships, and the Deprecation Bills Come Due
text:
# Node.js 26 'Lithium' Goes LTS: Temporal Ships, and the Deprecation Bills Come Due

Node.js 26.13.0 'Lithium' became Active LTS on October 28, with support to April 2029. Temporal by default, V8 14.6, real removals, and what upgrading a NestJS or Express service actually takes.

...

On October 28, Node.js 26.13.0 marked the transition of the 26.x line into Long Term Support under the codename "Lithium", with updates promised "through to the end of April 2029." The promotion changed nothing but metadata such as `process.release`; the substance arrived when 26.0.0 shipped as Current on May 5, a few days past the April slot the schedule had pencilled in. That release turned on Temporal by default, moved to V8 14.6, and finally removed APIs that have been printing warnings for years. It is also the last line cut under the old odd/even model, which makes it the LTS most teams will live on while the new annual cadence beds in.

## Temporal is a global now, and Date can start packing

The headline commit is five words long: build: enable Temporal by default. No flag, no import. Temporal splits what `Date` blurred into separate types, `Instant`, `ZonedDateTime`, `PlainDate`, `PlainTime`, `Duration` and the rest, and its design includes DST-safe arithmetic, which is the part your billing cron will quietly appreciate. The same engine bump, V8 14.6.202.33 from Chromium 146, adds `Map.prototype.getOrInsert()`, `getOrInsertComputed()` and `Iterator.concat()`. The snippet covers calendar math, a day versus 24 hours across a DST change, and both V8 additions:

...

One boundary to respect: MDN still labels Temporal limited availability, not Baseline, because some major browsers lack it. Use it freely in server code; in shared Next.js modules that also reach the client, keep a polyfill or a `globalThis.Temporal` guard.

...

Node 26 bundles undici 8.0.2, and InfoQ reports that `fetch()` needs no API changes. The Node notes describe no behavior changes, so treat it like any new major of your HTTP client: replay real outbound traffic, retries and connection pools included, through staging first.

...

The calendar sets the urgency. Per the Release Working Group schedule, Node 20 reached end of life on April 30, 2026. Node 22 has been in maintenance since October 21, 2025 and ends April 30, 2027. Node 24 entered maintenance on October 20, 2026 and ends April 30, 2028. Node 26 stays in Active LTS until October 20, 2027 and ends April 30, 2029. Counted from today, that leaves 171, 537 and 902 days of upstream support for 22, 24 and 26.

...

An LTS promotion is a ceremony, not a release. The real change happened in May, and the six months since were the project's way of letting the rest of us catch up. What sits within your control is small and mechanical: removed modules, a renamed option, a hook API, a crypto parameter, a Docker tag. What does not is how a new undici major behaves under your traffic and when Safari ships Temporal; for those, test and wait, respectively.

The larger shift is the calendar itself. Lithium is the last LTS chosen by parity. Node 27's first alpha was posted on October 29, and under the new schedule every major spends six months in Alpha, six as Current and 30 in LTS, so 27 itself becomes LTS in October 2027. One upgrade a year, on a 36-month horizon. The biennial chore becomes an annual habit, which is the better habit anyway: smaller jumps, fewer ancient warnings settled all at once.

title: Netlify Server is now available in Early Access
text:
Netlify Server lets you run your application’s backend as a long-lived Node.js server. Netlify provisions it, scales it with demand and scales it down to zero when nothing is using it.

...

Netlify Server keeps running between requests so that it can:

...

- Keep warm database connection pools and in-memory caches.
- Hold WebSocket and Server-Sent Events connections open, for things like live chat and real-time collaboration.

...

## Early Access

Netlify Server is available on credit-based plans and on Enterprise plans with credits enabled. Its APIs and behavior might change during Early Access.

In Agent Runners, we’re releasing Netlify Server gradually over the coming days, so your agent runs might not use it right away.

### Limits

These are the main limits during Early Access:

- A server scales up to 3 instances, or 1 instance on credit-based Free and Personal plans.
- An instance always scales to zero after 5 minutes without requests. After Early Access, you’ll be able to keep a minimum number of instances running, so infrequent requests won’t need to wait for your server to start.

The limits page has the full list.

### Pricing

Netlify Server is free to use during Early Access. When it reaches General Availability, usage will be charged in credits based on two meters: reserved memory (in GB-hours) and active CPU time (in vCPU-hours). We’ll announce the cost in credits before then. If your usage during Early Access suggests you’ll need to upgrade your plan or buy more credits, we’ll let you know.

Other metered features in your project are billed as usual, and every request your server handles counts toward the web requests meter. Learn more about pricing.

To get started, read the Netlify Server docs and follow the guide to create your first server.

title: Preparing Node.js Applications for the Next Generation of Web Infrastructure | nasscom | The Official Community of Indian IT Industry
text:
As JavaScript applications become more demanding, choosing nodejs hosting India involves more than selecting a server with sufficient processing power. Businesses need an environment that supports maintained runtimes, application compatibility, reliable deployments, efficient resource usage, and secure operations. With Node.js 26 entering Active Long-Term Support (LTS) on October 28, 2026, runtime selection and upgrade planning have become important considerations for development teams.

## Understand the Changing Node.js Runtime Landscape

Node.js releases introduce improvements to the JavaScript runtime, performance, security, and developer capabilities. However, adopting every new major version immediately is not always practical for production applications.

As of November 2026, Node.js 26 is in Active LTS, while versions 24 and 22 are in Maintenance LTS. Production teams should generally select a supported release that is compatible with their frameworks, packages, and deployment requirements.

...

Pin the runtime version in project configuration, test major upgrades in staging, and verify native dependencies before changing production environments.

title: Best Node.js Hosting In 2026 (7 Picks, From Free Tiers To Always-On Servers)
text:
Best Node.js Hosting In 2026 (7 Picks, From Free Tiers To Always-On Servers)

# Best Node.js Hosting In 2026 (7 Picks, From Free Tiers To Always-On Servers)

Istiak Rayhan

November 12, 2026

Node.js apps need a host that can run code all day, not just serve files. Some hosts do this for free with limits. Others charge a few dollars a month for an app that never sleeps.

We checked the official pricing pages of 7 Node.js hosts on November 12, 2026. Here is what each one really costs, and who should pick it.

## Quick answer

The best Node.js hosting for most people in 2026 is Render if you want a free start, and Railway if you want a simple paid plan from $5 a month. Fly.io is the cheapest always-on option at $2.19 a month for a 256 MB machine. If you also want email, a domain and a normal hosting panel, Hostinger runs Node.js apps from $2.79 a month (48-month term, renews at $16.99 a month).

## Node.js hosting compared (prices checked November 2026)

| Host | Best for | Starting price | Renewal / ongoing | Refund or trial |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Render | Free start, easy deploys | $0 (free tier), then $7/mo | Same price each month | Free tier, no refund window listed |
| Railway | Simple usage-based billing | $5/mo minimum (includes $5 usage) | Same each month, plus extra usage | 30-day free trial with $5 credit |
| Fly.io | Cheapest always-on app | $2.19/mo (256 MB) | Same each month | Short free trial, no card needed |
| DigitalOcean | Growing apps, full control | $5/mo App Platform, $4/mo Droplet | Same each month | No refund window listed |
| Hostinger | Node.js plus email and domain | $2.79/mo (48 months) | $16.99/mo | 30-day money-back |
| Heroku | Teams that like a classic PaaS | $5/mo (Eco), $7/mo (Basic) | Same each month | No free tier |
| Vercel | Next.js and serverless Node | $0 (Hobby, non-commercial) | Pro $20/mo per seat | Free Hobby plan |

Note: monthly cloud prices assume the app runs all month. Usage-based hosts can cost more if your app uses more memory, CPU or bandwidth.

...

We looked for hosts that can run a real Node.js server (Express, Fastify, NestJS, Next.js and similar). We checked each host’s official pricing page on November 12, 2026, and wrote down the first price, the ongoing price and any free tier or refund rules. We then sorted them by who they suit best, not by commission. A host had to be global and well known to make the list.

...

## 1. Render: best free start for Node.js

Render lets you connect a GitHub repo and deploy a Node.js web service in a few clicks. It is one of the few hosts that still has a free web service tier.

Prices (checked November 2026):

- Free web service: $0 a month, 512 MB RAM.
- Paid web service: $7 a month for 512 MB RAM, $25 a month for 1 CPU and 2 GB RAM.
- Workspace plan: Hobby is $0 plus compute. Pro is $25 a month plus compute.
- Postgres: free plan, or $6 a month for the smallest paid database.

Free tier limits: Render spins down a free web service after 15 minutes with no traffic. Waking it up takes about one minute. Each workspace gets 750 free instance hours per month. Free Postgres databases expire 30 days after you create them.

Pros:

- Real free tier for testing and side projects.
- Simple Git-based deploys and automatic HTTPS.
- Prices stay the same each month, with no promo jump.

Cons:

- Free apps sleep, so the first visit after a break is slow.
- The $25 Pro workspace fee adds up for small teams.

Pick this if: you want to launch a Node.js app for $0 today and move to $7 a month when it needs to stay awake.

## 2. Railway: best simple usage-based hosting

Railway is popular with developers who want to push code and not think about servers. You pay a small minimum, and that minimum is turned into usage credit.

Prices (checked November 2026):

- Free: 30-day trial with $5 of credit, then $1 a month. No credit card needed.
- Hobby: $5 minimum a month, which includes $5 of usage.
- Pro: $20 minimum a month, which includes $20 of usage.
- Usage rates: memory is $0.00000386 per GB per second, CPU is $0.00000772 per vCPU per second, and egress is $0.05 per GB.

In plain numbers, 1 GB of RAM running all month costs about $10, so a small app often fits inside or close to the $5 Hobby credit.

- Very easy deploys from GitHub, with databases in the same project.
- Your $5 minimum is not wasted, since it becomes usage.
- Scales up a lot on the same platform.

- Bills can grow if your app uses a lot of memory.
- The pricing page does not list a refund policy.

Pick this if: you want the easiest paid Node.js hosting, with a bill that starts at $5 a month.

## 3. Fly.io: cheapest always-on Node.js app

Fly.io runs your app inside small virtual machines. You can place them close to your users in many regions.

Prices (checked November 2026):

- shared-cpu-1x with 256 MB RAM: $2.19 a month.
- shared-cpu-1x with 512 MB RAM: $3.69 a month.
- shared-cpu-1x with 1 GB RAM: $6.70 a month.
- Paid support: Standard $29 a month, Premium $199 a month. Community support is free.
- Managed Postgres starts at $38 a month (Basic).

New accounts get a short free trial, and no credit card is needed to start. Fly.io’s docs say there is no ongoing free tier for new organizations.

- Lowest always-on price on this list.
- Easy to run your app in several regions.
- Billing is clear per machine size.

...

Pick this if: you are comfortable with a terminal and want an app that never sleeps for about $2 to $7 a month.

## 4. DigitalOcean: best for growing apps and full control

DigitalOcean gives you two ways to run Node.js. App Platform is a managed service like Render. Droplets are virtual servers you set up yourself.

Prices (checked November 2026):

- App Platform free tier: 3 static site apps for $0. (This is for static sites, not a Node.js server.)
- App Platform container: $5 a month for 1 vCPU, 512 MiB RAM and 50 GiB transfer. $10 a month for 1 GiB RAM.
- Basic Droplet: $4 a month for 1 vCPU, 512 MiB RAM, 10 GiB SSD and 500 GiB transfer. $6 a month for 1 GiB RAM.
- Development database on App Platform: $7 a month.

- Choice of managed (App Platform) or full control (Droplets).
- Fixed monthly prices with a monthly cap.
- Lots of tutorials for Node.js.

- A Droplet means you handle updates and security yourself.
- No free Node.js server tier.

Pick this if: you want a fixed $4 to $10 monthly bill and room to grow into bigger servers later.

...

## 5. Hostinger: best if you want Node.js plus email and a domain

Hostinger now supports Node.js apps on its web hosting plans, not just on VPS. This suits small business owners who want a website, email and an app in one place.

Prices (checked November 2026, Black Friday pricing shown on the site):

- Unlimited plan: $2.79 a month on a 48-month term ($133.92 paid today). Renews at $16.99 a month. Up to 5 web apps.
- Cloud Startup: $7.99 a month on a 48-month term ($383.52 paid today). Renews at $25.99 a month. Up to 10 web apps.
- KVM 1 VPS: $6.49 a month on a 24-month term ($155.76 paid today). Renews at $11.99 a month. 1 vCPU, 4 GB RAM.
- 30-day money-back guarantee on these plans.

The entry Premium plan does not list Node.js support, so start with Unlimited or higher.

- Node.js, email, a control panel and WordPress in one account.
- 30-day money-back guarantee.
- KVM 1 VPS gives 4 GB RAM for a low first-term price.

- Big jump at renewal (from $2.79 to $16.99 a month on Unlimited).
- You need a long term to get the lowest price.

Pick this if: you want a normal hosting account that can also run a Node.js app, and you are fine paying up front. Our guide to cutting hosting renewal costs shows how to soften the renewal jump.

## 6. Heroku: best classic platform for teams

Heroku was one of the first platforms where you could just push code. It is still a solid choice for teams that want a mature, well-documented setup.

Prices (checked November 2026):

- Eco dyno: $5 a month, 0.5 GB RAM. Personal accounts only. Sleeps after 30 minutes of no traffic.
- Basic dyno: $7 a month, 0.5 GB RAM, always on, free SSL.
- Standard-1X: $25 a month, 0.5 GB RAM, with zero-downtime deploys.
- Standard-2X: $50 a month, 1 GB RAM.

...

## 7. Vercel: best for Next.js and serverless Node

Vercel is built for frontend frameworks like Next.js. Your Node.js code runs as functions, not as one server that runs all day.

Prices (checked November 2026):

- Hobby: $0 a month, for personal and non-commercial use only.
- Pro: $20 a month per developer seat, including $20 of usage credit.
- Included on Pro: 4 hours of active CPU, 360 GB-hours of memory, 1 million function calls and 100 GB of fast data transfer per month.

...

## Who should choose what

- Just testing or learning: Render free tier (sleeps after 15 minutes idle).
- Simple paid hosting with little setup: Railway from $5 a month.
- Cheapest app that never sleeps: Fly.io from $2.19 a month.
- Fixed bill and room to grow: DigitalOcean from $4 a month (Droplet) or $5 a month (App Platform).
- Website, email and Node.js in one place: Hostinger from $2.79 a month (renews at $16.99).
- Teams that want a proven platform: Heroku from $7 a month for always-on.
- Next.js or serverless apps: Vercel, free for personal use, $20 a month for Pro.

...

DigitalOcean’s smallest Droplet is $4 a month, and Render’s always-on plan is $7 a month.

### Can I run Node.js on shared hosting?

Yes, some shared hosts now support it. Hostinger runs Node.js apps on its Unlimited plan ($2.79 a month for 48 months, renews at $16.99 a month) and higher plans. Shared hosting works for small apps, but busy apps do better on a VPS or a cloud platform.

...

## Update log

- November 2026: Published, using pricing checked on November 12, 2026.
